fatal_errors: The alloy is incorrectly assumed to be nanocrystalline; the target material is an as-cast, solidification-segregated dendritic alloy containing two BCC phases.

Grain-boundary sliding is asserted as the dominant mechanism without evidence and is inconsistent with the reported interpretations emphasizing solid-solution strengthening, lattice distortion, dislocation-related effects, localized plasticity, grain-boundary cohesion, and impeded crack propagation.
The proposed 800–1100 °C test regime lies outside the reported room-temperature-to-500 °C mechanical-testing range.
The prediction of lower alloy yield stress contradicts the observed higher strength: approximately 1.66 GPa versus 0.70 GPa at room temperature and 0.65 GPa versus 0.25 GPa at 500 °C.
The cited studies concern sputtered nanocrystalline W-Ta-V-Cr and CuMoTaWV films, not as-cast equimolar WTaTiVZr, and therefore do not establish its grain structure or deformation mechanism.
explanation: The response addresses the broad comparison of WTaTiVZr with tungsten and correctly anticipates improved plastic strain and toughness, but it reconstructs neither the actual material state nor the tested conditions. The central nanocrystalline grain-boundary-sliding hypothesis is imported from unrelated thin-film alloys and is not supported for the dendritic, dual-BCC as-cast alloy. Its controlled same-condition comparison and post-deformation TEM/EBSD could distinguish grain-boundary sliding from dislocation plasticity, but it would not isolate the proposed cause because composition, phase segregation, and grain size all differ simultaneously. It also omits the observed quantitative boundaries and outcomes, including approximately 6% room-temperature plastic strain, crack disappearance above 200 °C, greater than 20% indentation plastic strain at 500 °C, and scratch toughness of about 38 versus 25 MPa√m. The proposed mechanism is therefore a testable but presently unsupported alternative rather than a reconstruction of the target.
